script: NBA players who won a title, but still forced their way out of town. The Milwaukee Bucks once drafted a 7-foot-2 kid out of UCLA with the very first pick back in 1969. His name was Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. And in just his second season, he handed Milwaukee its first ever championship. He won three MVP awards there, so he was already one of the best players the sport had ever seen, and he did it all in a tiny market. But the trophy he lifted was the exact thing that told him it was time to go. Right before the 1974 season started, Kareem quietly walked into the Bucks front office and asked to be traded. He didn't leak it to the press or cause a scene, he just told them privately so they could get the best deal possible behind closed doors. It wasn't about basketball for him, because a New York kid at heart, he said his lifestyle and Milwaukee's lifestyle simply didn't match. He wanted a bigger stage, and he named his spots: New York, Los Angeles, or Washington. But the city sitting at the very top of his list is the one he never got. Reports had him headed to the Knicks, but instead, on June 16th, 1975, Milwaukee shipped him to the Los Angeles Lakers for four players, and New York never happened. And here's the wild part. In Los Angeles, Kareem won five more championships and became the all-time leading scorer in NBA history, finishing his career with 38,387 points, a record that stood for almost 40 years.
